prompt: Which of these treats light as a straight-line traveler best suited for everyday lens design?
explanation: Geometric (ray) optics ignores the wave nature of light and treats it as straight lines. It works whenever wavelengths are much smaller than the optical components — true for almost all camera and telescope design.

prompt: What is the wavelength (in nm) of light with frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz? (Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.)
explanation: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸) / (6 × 10¹⁴) = 5 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. That's green light, near the peak of human visual sensitivity.

prompt: The photoelectric effect demonstrated that:
options: Light has no detectable rest mass
Light always travels at speed c
explanation: Einstein's 1905 explanation: a photon must individually have enough energy (E = hf) to eject an electron. Below a threshold frequency, no electrons come out no matter how bright the light. This forced light to have a particle aspect alongside its wave aspect.

prompt: Visible light wavelengths are roughly 400 to 700 nanometers.
explanation: Yes — about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Below 400 nm is ultraviolet; above 700 nm is infrared. Both are invisible to humans but seen by other animals (bees see UV, snakes see IR).

prompt: Match the picture of light to the situation where it dominates:
explanation: Each picture is correct in its regime. Use rays when the optical path is large compared to the wavelength, waves when interference matters, photons when discrete energy exchanges matter.

prompt: Snell's law describes:
options: How light reflects from a mirror
How a wave bends at a media boundary
How a photon's energy is changed
Why the daytime sky appears blue
correctAnswer: How a wave bends at a media boundary
explanation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. The bending happens because light travels at different speeds in different media; the refractive index n = c/v captures the slowdown.

prompt: Why does a fiber optic cable carry light over kilometers without leaking?
options: Modern lasers don't lose energy at all
Light somehow bends around the cable
explanation: Above the critical angle, light hitting the core/cladding boundary reflects entirely back into the core. With proper geometry, all the light that enters comes out the far end — the basis of long-haul fiber optic communication.

prompt: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a lens with focal length 10 cm. Where is the image (in cm, positive = real image on the other side)?
explanation: 1/d_i = 1/f − 1/d_o = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so d_i = 15 cm. The image is real, inverted, and reduced (magnification = −15/30 = −0.5).

prompt: Light entering a glass block (n = 1.5) from air (n = 1):
options: Speeds up and bends away from the normal
Slows down and bends toward the normal
Keeps the same speed but changes color
correctAnswer: Slows down and bends toward the normal
explanation: Higher index = slower speed. By Snell's law, going from low n to high n bends the ray toward the normal. This is why a pencil in water looks bent — the rays from the underwater part bend on exit.

prompt: A diverging lens always produces a virtual image smaller than the object.
explanation: For any object position, a diverging (concave) lens forms an upright, virtual, reduced image on the same side as the object. This is why peephole lenses in doors give a wide-angle view — they're diverging.

prompt: Bright fringes in Young's double-slit experiment occur where:
options: At the widest slits in the array
Where path difference is half lambda
Where light is most intense at source
explanation: Constructive interference requires d sin θ = mλ. Crests aligning with crests give maximum brightness. Path differences of (m + ½)λ instead cancel completely (dark fringes).

prompt: If you narrow a single slit, the central diffraction peak:
explanation: First dark fringe at sin θ = λ/a. Smaller a → larger θ → wider central maximum. This is why a tiny aperture (pinhole camera) creates a fuzzy image rather than a sharp one.

prompt: Why do CDs and DVDs show rainbow colors?
options: The disc plastic is dyed colourfully
Data tracks act as a diffraction grating
The reading laser leaves a residue
correctAnswer: Data tracks act as a diffraction grating
explanation: The data tracks are spaced about a wavelength of light apart, forming a diffraction grating. Each color exits at a different angle; tilt the disc and the rainbow shifts.

prompt: Diffraction gratings make spectral lines sharper than a simple two-slit interferometer.
explanation: Many slits acting in concert sharpen the constructive maxima dramatically — peaks become very narrow. This is why spectrometers use gratings, not just two slits.

prompt: Match the phenomenon to its cause:
explanation: All three are wave-optics effects — they vanish in the ray-optics limit. Wavelength-scale geometry is what reveals light's wave nature.

prompt: Polarized sunglasses reduce glare from a horizontal road because:
options: The lenses are simply tinted dark
Glare is horizontal; lens blocks it
They block ultraviolet only, not glare
They reflect everything that hits them
correctAnswer: Glare is horizontal; lens blocks it
explanation: Light reflecting off a horizontal surface tends to come out polarized horizontally (Brewster's angle is exact, near-Brewster is strongly preferential). A vertical-axis polarizer cuts that glare without dimming everything else equally.

prompt: Unpolarized light of intensity I₀ passes through a polarizer. What is the output intensity?
explanation: An ideal polarizer transmits exactly half of unpolarized light, and the transmitted light is polarized along its axis. Each polarizer downstream then follows Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ.

prompt: Stimulated emission produces a photon that is:
options: Random in direction and in phase
Higher in energy than the trigger
explanation: That cloning is what makes lasers coherent. Each new photon is a copy of the trigger; the cascade through the gain medium produces an avalanche of identical photons.

prompt: Why must a laser have a population inversion?
options: So gravity won't pull photons down
To filter out the wrong colours of light
explanation: In thermal equilibrium more atoms are in the ground state, and a photon is more likely to be absorbed than to stimulate emission. Pumping creates an inverted population so net amplification can happen.

prompt: A laser pointer makes a small bright spot kilometers away because its light is coherent and well-collimated.
explanation: Same wavelength, same direction, same phase — and beam divergence is set only by diffraction. A flashlight, by contrast, spreads in all directions and dilutes quickly with distance.

prompt: What does a hologram record that a photograph does not?
explanation: A photograph records intensity only. A hologram records the interference pattern of object and reference beams — that pattern encodes the full wavefront, including phase, which is what gives the reconstructed image its 3D depth.

prompt: Wavelength-division multiplexing in fiber optics works by:
options: Splitting one beam into two beams
explanation: Different wavelengths don't interfere with each other in a linear medium, so dozens of colors can ride the same fiber at once. Modern systems carry tens of terabits per second per fiber this way.

prompt: Frequency doubling in a nonlinear crystal turns infrared into:
explanation: A 1064 nm IR laser doubled in KTP becomes 532 nm green — the basis of green laser pointers. Frequency doubling is a nonlinear effect that requires high intensities and a non-centrosymmetric crystal.

prompt: Quantum cryptography uses single-photon properties to detect any eavesdropping on a key exchange.
explanation: Protocols like BB84 encode bits in photon polarizations or phases. Any measurement disturbs them (no-cloning theorem), so an eavesdropper inevitably introduces detectable errors.

prompt: Match the technology to its underlying principle:

pairs.right: Frequency doubling in a nonlinear crystal

explanation: Modern photonics is built from a small number of physical principles repeated in different combinations. Each of these technologies relies on a different one.
